title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: On the Pratzen Heights, where he had fallen with the flagstaff in his hand, Prince Andrew Bolkonski lay bleeding heavily, unconsciously letting out a gentle, pitiful, childlike moan.
Toward evening he stopped moaning and became completely still. He had no idea how long he had been unconscious. Suddenly he felt alive again, aware of a burning, tearing pain in his head.

"Where is it, that vast sky I never knew until now, but saw today?" was his first thought. "And I never knew this suffering either," he thought. "Yes, I knew nothing, absolutely nothing until now. But where am I?"

He listened and heard the sound of horses approaching, along with voices speaking French. He opened his eyes. Above him was the same vast sky with clouds that had risen higher still, and between them shone an endless blue infinity. He did not turn his head and did not see those who, judging by the hoofbeats and voices, had ridden up and stopped near him.

It was Napoleon, accompanied by two aides-de-camp. Bonaparte, riding across the battlefield, had given final orders to strengthen the batteries firing at the Augesd Dam, and was now surveying the dead and wounded left on the field.
"Fine men!" Napoleon remarked, looking at a dead Russian grenadier who lay facedown with a blackened neck, one stiffened arm flung wide.
"The ammunition for the guns in position is exhausted, Your Majesty," said an adjutant who had come from the batteries firing at Augesd.

"Have some brought from the reserve," said Napoleon, and having walked on a few steps, he stopped before Prince Andrew, who lay on his back with the flagstaff dropped beside him. (The flag itself had already been taken by the French as a trophy.)
"That's a fine death!" said Napoleon, gazing at Bolkonski.

Prince Andrew understood that this was said about him and that it was Napoleon who said it. He heard the speaker addressed as Sire. But he heard the words the way one might hear the buzzing of a fly. Not only did they not interest him — he paid no attention to them at all and immediately forgot them. His head was burning, he felt himself bleeding to death, and he saw above him the distant, vast, everlasting sky. He knew it was Napoleon — his hero — but at that moment Napoleon seemed to him such a small, insignificant creature compared with what was happening now between himself and that vast infinite sky with its drifting clouds. At that moment it meant nothing to him who might be standing over him or what was said of him. He was only glad that people were near him, and he only wished they would help him and bring him back to life, which now seemed so beautiful, since today he had learned to see it so differently. He gathered all his strength, trying to stir and make a sound. He weakly moved his leg and let out a faint, sickly groan that aroused his own pity.
"Ah! He is alive," said Napoleon. "Lift this young man up and carry him to the dressing station."
Having said this, Napoleon rode on to meet Marshal Lannes, who, hat in hand, rode up smiling to the Emperor to congratulate him on the victory.

Prince Andrew remembered nothing more: he lost consciousness from the terrible pain of being lifted onto the stretcher, the jolting while being carried, and the probing of his wound at the dressing station. He did not regain consciousness until late in the day, when he was carried along with other wounded and captured Russian officers to the hospital. During this transfer he felt a little stronger and was able to look around and even speak.

The first words he heard on coming to his senses were from a French convoy officer, who said rapidly: "We must stop here: the Emperor will pass this way shortly, and it will please him to see these prisoners."
"There are so many prisoners today — nearly the whole Russian army — he's probably tired of them," said another officer.
"All the same! They say this one is the commander of all Emperor Alexander's Guards," said the first, pointing to a Russian officer in the white uniform of the Horse Guards.
Bolkonski recognized Prince Repnin, whom he had met in Petersburg society. Beside him stood a nineteen-year-old boy, also a wounded officer of the Horse Guards.
Bonaparte came galloping up and pulled his horse to a stop.
"Which is the senior?" he asked, seeing the prisoners.
They named the colonel, Prince Repnin.
"You are the commander of Emperor Alexander's Horse Guards regiment?" asked Napoleon.
"I commanded a squadron," replied Repnin.
"Your regiment fulfilled its duty honorably," said Napoleon.
"The praise of a great commander is a soldier's highest reward," said Repnin.
"I give it with pleasure," said Napoleon. "And who is that young man beside you?"
Prince Repnin named Lieutenant Sukhtelen.
After looking at him, Napoleon smiled.
"He's very young to come meddling with us."
"Youth is no obstacle to courage," Sukhtelen muttered in a failing voice.
"A splendid reply!" said Napoleon. "Young man, you will go far!"

Prince Andrew, who had also been brought forward before the Emperor's eyes to complete the display of prisoners, could not fail to attract his attention. Napoleon apparently remembered seeing him on the battlefield and, addressing him, again used the phrase "young man" that was connected in his memory with Prince Andrew.
"Well, and you, young man," he said. "How do you feel, mon brave?"

Though five minutes earlier Prince Andrew had been able to say a few words to the soldiers carrying him, now with his eyes fixed straight on Napoleon, he was silent. So insignificant at that moment seemed all the interests that consumed Napoleon, so petty did his hero himself appear with his trivial vanity and delight in victory, compared to the vast, fair, and kindly sky he had seen and understood, that he could not answer him.

Everything seemed so pointless and insignificant compared to the solemn chain of thoughts that weakness from blood loss, suffering, and the nearness of death stirred in him. Looking into Napoleon's eyes, Prince Andrew reflected on the insignificance of greatness, the unimportance of life which no one could understand, and the still greater unimportance of death, the meaning of which no living person could comprehend or explain.

The Emperor, without waiting for an answer, turned away and said to one of his officers as he left: "Have these gentlemen attended to and taken to my bivouac. Let my doctor, Larrey, examine their wounds. Farewell, Prince Repnin!" And he spurred his horse and galloped away.
His face glowed with self-satisfaction and pleasure.

The soldiers who had carried Prince Andrew had noticed the little gold icon Princess Mary had hung around her brother's neck, and they had taken it. But seeing how the Emperor favored the prisoners, they now hurried to return the holy image.
Prince Andrew did not see how or by whom it was put back, but the little icon with its thin gold chain suddenly appeared on his chest outside his uniform.

"It would be good," thought Prince Andrew, glancing at the icon his sister had hung around his neck with such feeling and devotion, "it would be good if everything were as clear and simple as it seems to Mary. How wonderful it would be to know where to seek help in this life, and what to expect after it, beyond the grave! How happy and at peace I would be if I could now say: 'Lord, have mercy on me!' But to whom should I say that? Either to a Power indefinable, incomprehensible, which I cannot even address, let alone put into words — the Great All or Nothing," he said to himself, "or to that God who has been sewn into this amulet by Mary! There is nothing certain, nothing at all — except the unimportance of everything I understand, and the greatness of something incomprehensible but supremely important."

The stretchers moved on. At every jolt he felt unbearable pain again; his fever rose and he became delirious. Visions of his father, his wife, his sister, and his future son, the tenderness he had felt the night before the battle, the figure of the insignificant little Napoleon, and above all the vast sky — these became the main subjects of his fevered imaginings.

The quiet domestic life and peaceful happiness of Bald Hills appeared before him. He was already enjoying that happiness when that little Napoleon had suddenly appeared with his unsympathetic expression of narrow-minded delight at others' misery, and doubts and torments had followed, and only the heavens promised peace. Toward morning all these dreams dissolved and merged into the chaos and darkness of unconsciousness and oblivion, which in the opinion of Napoleon's doctor, Larrey, was far more likely to end in death than in recovery.
"He is a nervous, bilious subject," said Larrey, "and will not recover."
And Prince Andrew, along with others who were fatally wounded, was left to the care of the local inhabitants.
